articles.headline: Rep. Lawler Criticizes Congestion Pricing While Constituents Face Higher Gas Costs
articles.dek: While calling congestion pricing a "cash grab," Representative Mike Lawler has downplayed the impact of rising gas prices on his constituents, which have exceeded congestion toll costs.
articles.lead: Representative Mike Lawler has voiced strong opposition to New York's congestion pricing program, labeling it a "cash grab" during a recent interview. However, Lawler has been less concerned about the significant increase in gasoline prices experienced by his constituents in the Hudson Valley.
articles.takeaway: While calling congestion pricing a "cash grab," Representative Mike Lawler has downplayed the impact of rising gas prices on his constituents, which have exceeded congestion toll costs.
body: Representative Mike Lawler has voiced strong opposition to New York's congestion pricing program, labeling it a "cash grab" during a recent interview. However, Lawler has been less concerned about the significant increase in gasoline prices experienced by his constituents in the Hudson Valley.

Gas prices have surged due to disruptions in oil shipments from the Middle East, a situation exacerbated by recent geopolitical events. Since late February, households in Lawler's district have reportedly spent an additional $102 million on gasoline, averaging $390 per household. This figure surpasses the $58 million paid in congestion charges since the program began in early 2025.

Lawler, whose district includes Rockland, Putnam, and parts of Dutchess and Westchester counties, stated that gas prices are volatile and expected to decrease. He has repeatedly criticized congestion pricing, arguing it is not about reducing traffic or environmental concerns but solely about revenue generation.

In contrast to his stance on congestion pricing, Lawler has supported military actions that have contributed to the rise in fuel costs. The increased cost of gasoline due to these events is estimated to be hitting the district's households five times harder daily than congestion tolls.

While congestion pricing revenues are intended to fund public transit improvements, including station accessibility and signal upgrades, the increased cost of gasoline due to geopolitical factors has placed a larger financial burden on Lawler's constituents. The analysis suggests that the district's reliance on cars contributes significantly to their higher fuel expenses.

body: Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations A city investigation published Thursday found a yellow bus carrying six nonverbal autistic students in Brooklyn was lost for more than four hours on the way to school last year while a panicked group of parents and school officials struggled to locate the children.

The report by the Special Commissioner of Investigation, a watchdog agency for the city’s public schools, said a bus operated by Consolidated Bus Transit was scheduled to arrive at a Brooklyn elementary school before 9 a.m.

on Dec. 16, but did not show up until 1:25 p.m. that day. Parents tried to track the bus’s winding route via AirTags placed in their children’s backpacks while school staff struggled to reach the bus company, the investigation found.

When the bus of 6- to 8-year-olds did arrive, one student was lying in a pool of urine, according to the report. It’s the latest in a string of incidents that have parents and regulators calling for urgent reforms to the city’s dysfunctional school bus system.
While the majority of New York’s students walk, drive or take public transit to school, about 155,000 rely on yellow buses. Half of those using the buses have disabilities.

Parents have long complained of delays, circuitous routes, broken GPS systems and unresponsive call center staff. They said improving the bus system will require passing legislation in Albany so the city can rebid and replace 45-year-old bus contracts with new contracts that add strict requirements for vendors and strengthen service for students.

articles.takeaway: Find our headlines more quickly in Google search results.
body: Find our headlines more quickly in Google search results. Mayor Zohran Mamdani appointed Liz Vladeck, the Department of Education’s top lawyer, to lead his Office of Labor Relations — a crucial role tasked with representing the city in collective bargaining with unions representing hundreds of thousands of teachers, law enforcement, first responders and other civil servants.
Vladeck will succeed Commissioner Renee Campion, who this summer made the surprise announcement of her retirement effective Dec. 1, after nearly a quarter century at the agency.

She will stay on as commissioner until that date, a City Hall source said. Vladeck will have a lengthy to-do list. The Mamdani administration is in the middle of negotiating funding for a health program that pays for civil servants’ prescription drugs, chemotherapy and other benefits.

Money for that program, known as PICA, was tied up in a cash pot that was declared insolvent days before Mamdani’s inauguration. Those talks are the main obstacle to beginning negotiations on a new contract covering members of District Council 37, the city’s largest public sector union with approximately 100,000 members, sources have told The City Reporter.
The current contract expires next month. “Public servants keep our city running and they deserve respect, support, and a City government that takes its responsibilities to them seriously.
I look forward to looking closely with Liz and our city’s unions to deliver real results for New Yorkers across the five boroughs,” Mamdani said in a statement.

articles.headline: Man Accused of Giving Fentanyl to College Students, Leading to One Death
articles.dek: Federal prosecutors allege Moises Freire provided a substance he claimed was cocaine, but was actually fentanyl, to two women at a Manhattan dorm, resulting in one fatality and one overdose.
articles.lead: Moises Freire is facing federal charges for allegedly providing fentanyl to two college students in a Manhattan dorm room, a substance he described in a message as "straight poison" after it made him sick. Prosecutors claim Freire presented the drug as "pure cocaine" to the women, leading to both losing consciousness. One woman later died in a hospital, while the other survived.
articles.takeaway: Federal prosecutors allege Moises Freire provided a substance he claimed was cocaine, but was actually fentanyl, to two women at a Manhattan dorm, resulting in one fatality and one overdose.
body: Moises Freire is facing federal charges for allegedly providing fentanyl to two college students in a Manhattan dorm room, a substance he described in a message as "straight poison" after it made him sick. Prosecutors claim Freire presented the drug as "pure cocaine" to the women, leading to both losing consciousness. One woman later died in a hospital, while the other survived.

Freire was indicted on drug-related charges along with Brian Peralta Cabrera, who prosecutors accuse of supplying the fentanyl to Freire. The indictment does not specify the university, but Freire's attorney indicated it occurred at the Fashion Institute of Technology.

Prosecutors allege Freire pressured the women to use the drugs on March 18. Freire reportedly admitted to campus security that he had been with one of the women and found her unconscious afterward. He also stated he saw the other woman on the floor with her eyes rolled back.

Freire is accused of texting friends about the women's condition and sending photos while they were unconscious, waiting at least 40 minutes before seeking help. His attorney argued that Freire was not a drug dealer and that the women invited him over and asked for cocaine, describing the events as "dumb teenager things."

articles.headline: Enrollment Drops in NYC’s Healthcare Safety Net Amid Immigrant Fears
articles.dek: People walk through Bellevue Hospital, April 7, 2026. Credit: Alex Krales/THE CITY Enrollment in a city-run program designed to provide health access to New Yorkers ineligible for insurance, including undocumented resid…
articles.lead: People walk through Bellevue Hospital, April 7, 2026. Credit: Alex Krales/THE CITY Enrollment in a city-run program designed to provide health access to New Yorkers ineligible for insurance, including undocumented residents, continues to decline.
articles.takeaway: People walk through Bellevue Hospital, April 7, 2026.
body: People walk through Bellevue Hospital, April 7, 2026. Credit: Alex Krales/THE CITY Enrollment in a city-run program designed to provide health access to New Yorkers ineligible for insurance, including undocumented residents, continues to decline.
The number of people signed up for NYC Care decreased 12% from 140,222 patients in fiscal 2025 to 123,124 in fiscal 2026, according to the latest Mayor’s Management Report.

The program has served as a medical lifeline for some of the city’s immigrants who are excluded from Medicaid and other public programs. “It’s always alarming and very concerning to see drops in enrollment in healthcare, right?

Especially for vulnerable populations,” City Councilmember Alexa Avilés, who serves on the committee for immigration, told The City Reporter. NYC Health + Hospitals, which administers NYC Care, blamed the drop on a combination of factors: aging participants transitioning to Medicaid regardless of their immigration status; expansion of Medicaid and Child Health Plus; and continuous Medicaid eligibility for children under the age of six.

A busy entrance at Woodhull Hospital in Bushwick, Brooklyn, Jan. 22, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/THE CITY Still, the agency is hearing “anecdotally” of an “increasing reluctance” by immigrants to hand over basic information needed to enroll due to fears it could be handed over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to the yearly management report.
“Immigrants in particular are definitely fearful as they see the federal government taking data from other agencies where historically they did not do that,” Avilés said.

articles.dek: Over 100 elected officials, led by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have signed a letter asking private parking lot owners in New York City to refuse access to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
articles.lead: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and more than 100 New York state elected officials are calling on private parking lot and garage owners across the five boroughs to prohibit U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from using their properties. The officials released a letter Friday urging owners not to rent, lend, or otherwise make their property available to ICE for immigration enforcement staging grounds.
articles.takeaway: Over 100 elected officials, led by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have signed a letter asking private parking lot owners in New York City to refuse access to U.S.
body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and more than 100 New York state elected officials are calling on private parking lot and garage owners across the five boroughs to prohibit U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from using their properties. The officials released a letter Friday urging owners not to rent, lend, or otherwise make their property available to ICE for immigration enforcement staging grounds.

The letter highlights a recent incident where ICE officers shot and wounded an immigrant in Marble Hill, near a parking lot that local officials stated ICE had been using as a staging area. The signatories emphasized that such use of private property can place owners, employees, and customers at the center of controversial enforcement actions.

Among the officials who signed the letter are New York's two senators, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, City Council Speaker Julie Menin, and a majority of the City Council. The initiative targets the use of private lots, including specific instances on Northern Boulevard in Queens and Morton Street in Lower Manhattan, where protests have previously occurred.

This push follows actions by other entities, such as the owner of the Morton Street garage, who ended their contract with ICE after local protests. The Hudson River Park Trust also let its parking contract with the Department of Homeland Security expire in June after public outcry. The city government has also taken steps to ensure its own properties are not used for federal immigration enforcement, in line with sanctuary laws.

articles.headline: MTA Labels Transit Upgrades as Funded by Congestion Pricing
articles.dek: New signage highlights how revenue from Manhattan's vehicle-tolling program is financing significant improvements to the subway system, including accessibility upgrades.
articles.lead: The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) has begun placing "Made Possible by Congestion Pricing" signs on transit upgrades funded by the Manhattan vehicle-tolling program. The initiative aims to raise billions for capital improvements by charging drivers entering the city's congested core.
articles.takeaway: New signage highlights how revenue from Manhattan's vehicle-tolling program is financing significant improvements to the subway system, including accessibility upgrades.
body: The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) has begun placing "Made Possible by Congestion Pricing" signs on transit upgrades funded by the Manhattan vehicle-tolling program. The initiative aims to raise billions for capital improvements by charging drivers entering the city's congested core.

Four new elevators being installed at the 42nd Street–Bryant Park/Fifth Avenue subway complex are the first to be identified with these signs. MTA Chairperson and CEO Janno Lieber stated that the signage helps riders understand how their money is being used and the benefits they receive from the transit system.

Revenue from the congestion relief zone, which covers the area south of 60th Street, is contributing $15 billion to the MTA's capital plan for 2020-2024. This funding is earmarked for major projects including the East Harlem extension of the Second Avenue Subway, signal upgrades, and accessibility improvements at over 20 stations.

The accessibility upgrades at the 42nd Street–Bryant Park station, which serves over 100,000 riders daily, will bring the station into compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. This includes adding three elevators to connect street level to platforms on multiple lines, addressing previous issues with low availability rates of privately maintained elevators at the station.

Further enhancements at the Bryant Park hub, expected by late 2028, will include rebuilding platforms, installing new fare gates, and overhauling restrooms. Similar ADA upgrades funded by congestion pricing are also underway at 23 other stations across the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens, as the MTA aims to make 95% of its stations accessible by 2055.

articles.headline: National Grid Customers in NYC to Face Higher Gas Bills This Winter
articles.dek: Delivery costs, approved by the state in 2024, are the primary driver of the increase, despite lower commodity prices.
articles.lead: National Grid customers in parts of Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island can expect an increase in their natural gas bills this winter. Approximately 1.2 million customers will see their bills rise by an average of $87 over five months, from November through March, compared to last year.
articles.takeaway: Delivery costs, approved by the state in 2024, are the primary driver of the increase, despite lower commodity prices.
body: National Grid customers in parts of Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island can expect an increase in their natural gas bills this winter. Approximately 1.2 million customers will see their bills rise by an average of $87 over five months, from November through March, compared to last year.

While the cost of natural gas itself is projected to be lower this winter than in the previous year, the overall bill increase is attributed to higher delivery costs. These delivery costs, which cover the maintenance and operation of the gas network, were approved by the state in 2024 and are set to increase by an average of $211 over the same five-month period.

National Grid spokesperson Brian Sapp noted that these figures are approximate and subject to change based on weather conditions and energy usage. He recalled that last winter's colder-than-normal temperatures led to higher-than-forecasted bills due to increased consumption.

Customers on Long Island and the Rockaways will experience a smaller average increase of $5 for the entire winter season. This is because the delivery charges for the roughly 570,000 customers in these areas will rise by a more modest $125 over the season.

These delivery charge increases are part of a rate process overseen by the state's Public Service Commission and include costs for upgrading aging infrastructure and expanding capacity. For customers facing financial difficulties, National Grid New York President Matt Barnett highlighted state programs like the Home Energy Assistance Program, which opens next month, and nearly $300 million in available bill discounts for downstate customers.

articles.headline: Brooklyn School Dean Alleges Assault by MTA Fare Inspectors
articles.dek: A dean at Mott Bridges Academy claims MTA EAGLE unit officers assaulted him over a disputed $3 bus fare, leading to injuries and a planned lawsuit.
articles.lead: Kyle Taylor, a dean at Mott Bridges Academy in Brownsville, stated that MTA fare inspectors stopped him on a B14 bus on October 6, demanding proof of fare payment. Taylor claims he had paid using a paper transfer ticket, but inspectors on the sidewalk apprehended him as he attempted to exit the bus.
articles.takeaway: A dean at Mott Bridges Academy claims MTA EAGLE unit officers assaulted him over a disputed $3 bus fare, leading to injuries and a planned lawsuit.
body: Kyle Taylor, a dean at Mott Bridges Academy in Brownsville, stated that MTA fare inspectors stopped him on a B14 bus on October 6, demanding proof of fare payment. Taylor claims he had paid using a paper transfer ticket, but inspectors on the sidewalk apprehended him as he attempted to exit the bus.

Video footage shared by Taylor's attorney appears to show him struggling with inspectors who allegedly pinned him against the bus, slammed him against a shelter, and knocked him to the ground. An NYPD officer intervened to break up the incident. Taylor reported being taken to the hospital by ambulance and sustaining injuries to his back, neck, shoulder, arm, and elbow, preventing him from returning to work.

An NYPD complaint summary, however, alleges Taylor "fell out of the bus" and refused medical attention, a claim Taylor's account and the video footage contradict. Taylor intends to sue the MTA, whose representatives declined to comment due to pending litigation.

The incident occurs amidst an MTA crackdown on fare evasion, which officials estimate costs the agency over $300 million annually. Fare evasion on buses reportedly increased in the first half of 2026, a period marked by Mayor Zohran Mamdani's pledge to make buses "fast and free."

MTA Chair Janno Lieber has indicated plans to increase fare evasion enforcement, suggesting the EAGLE team could use devices to verify OMNY payments, the sole accepted method after MetroCards were discontinued in June. Taylor's attorney, Benjamin Pinczewski, argued that such enforcement disproportionately affects riders of color, citing NYPD data showing high percentages of fare evasion summonses and arrests among this demographic in early 2026.

Taylor and advocates are calling for the dismissal of the involved inspectors and the equipping of the unit with body cameras, similar to NYPD officers. Civil rights activist Rev. Kevin McCall urged Governor Kathy Hochul to investigate the unit and state lawmakers to mandate body cameras for its inspectors.

articles.headline: Lose-Lose? Bay Ridge Pol Celebrates More Parking, Less Housing
articles.dek: A Brooklyn City Council member claimed victory after she got developers of a potential housing site adjacent to a subway to reduce the number of units and add far more on-site parking than city law requires — a lose-los…
articles.lead: A Brooklyn City Council member claimed victory after she got developers of a potential housing site adjacent to a subway to reduce the number of units and add far more on-site parking than city law requires — a lose-lose for the neighborhood.
articles.takeaway: A Brooklyn City Council member claimed victory after she got developers of a potential housing site adjacent to a subway to reduce the number of units and add far more on-site parking than city law requires — a lose-los…
body: A Brooklyn City Council member claimed victory after she got developers of a potential housing site adjacent to a subway to reduce the number of units and add far more on-site parking than city law requires — a lose-lose for the neighborhood.

Council Member Kayla Santosuosso (D-Bay Ridge) took to X last week to brag about securing what she dubbed “major benefits” — specifically, a commitment from the developer to build fewer units of housing (and fewer below-market-rate “affordable” units) plus 200 parking spaces, which is 170 more than city law requires.
So instead of 292 new units — with 88 priced below market rate — in the neighborhood, the negotiated building will have 273 units and 82 units with slightly better affordability levels.

Santosuosso declared victory for the neighborhood because the resulting units will be bigger, and more suitable for families, compared to the original proposal, which would have had more one bedroom apartments and less parking, according to a CPC presentation.

But Santosuosso’s celebration is misguided at best, according to experts, because the cost of building parking is typically so high that developers typically reduce the number of units — and raise each unit’s price — to compensate.

“The decision of increasing the parking requirements, and claiming that as a victory, is really contrary to our own research that shows that [increasing required parking] has ultimately a larger scale negative effect on the availability of housing and how affordable that housing is,” said Marcel Negret, director of land use at the Regional Plan Association, who authored a report on the effect of parking requirements on affordable housing.

Tuesday marked the first school day this year the school didn’t have the fences up, and two security guards assumed crossing guard roles before school and at dismissal to ensure safety of students.

articles.headline: Man Shot by ICE Agents Claims They Did Not Identify Themselves
articles.dek: A new court filing alleges federal immigration agents approached Oscar Belgal's vehicle with firearms drawn and masked, contradicting official accounts.
articles.lead: Oscar Belgal, who was shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Marble Hill, claims the officers never identified themselves before opening fire. Belgal's attorneys filed a petition in Brooklyn federal court stating that masked agents approached his vehicle with weapons drawn and did not communicate with him.
articles.takeaway: A new court filing alleges federal immigration agents approached Oscar Belgal's vehicle with firearms drawn and masked, contradicting official accounts.
body: Oscar Belgal, who was shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Marble Hill, claims the officers never identified themselves before opening fire. Belgal's attorneys filed a petition in Brooklyn federal court stating that masked agents approached his vehicle with weapons drawn and did not communicate with him.

This account contradicts statements from U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, who said agents identified themselves during the Oct. 8 encounter. The petition also asserts that Belgal vehemently denies any affiliation with gangs or organized criminal groups, a claim made by ICE and DHS officials as justification for his arrest.

The petition further states that Belgal was not attempting to ram his vehicle into officers, as federal officials claimed. Instead, his attorneys argue video footage shows he was trying to move away from the agent firing into his car. After being shot in the neck, Belgal pleaded for medical assistance, but the petition alleges agents handcuffed him and left him without aid, with NYPD officers eventually taking him to receive medical care.

Belgal did not realize the individuals were ICE agents until he woke up in the hospital. The petition details the trauma experienced by Belgal and his son, who reportedly suffers from nightmares. Belgal is currently in ICE custody, and a federal judge has ordered he not be removed from the country or transferred outside the New York City metro area or New Jersey.

body: Find our headlines more quickly in Google search results. The Dominican man shot by an immigration agent in Marble Hill was arrested without a valid warrant and is being held in solitary confinement without proper medical care, according to a new court filing submitted by his attorneys Wednesday afternoon.

Oscar Belgal had just picked up his son from school then taken him to McDonald’s when plainclothes Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents rushed his car and fired at least seven shots, striking him in the neck.

Belgal identified an “anonymous, masked man,” who first approached his drivers-side window with a gun drawn, The Legal Aid Society wrote in court papers.The agent then “struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat.” Video of the incident released by the New York Police Department, shows a man in a grey sweatshirt and a red hat as the first to approach Belgal’s SUV and bang on the window.
The identity of the shooter has still not been confirmed by federal authorities. “After ICE shot him, Oscar exited his vehicle and pleaded for medical assistance, fearing that he was dying.
And believing the same, his son began yelling that the masked individuals had killed his dad,” the petition reads. Sign up for free morning headlines in your inbox.

articles.headline: New York Joins Federal Private School Tax Credit Program
articles.dek: Governor Hochul announced the state will participate in a federal scholarship tax credit program, aiming to generate funds for public school students.
articles.lead: Governor Kathy Hochul announced Friday that New York will opt into a federal scholarship tax credit program, a move she believes will bring millions of dollars to the state for public school students. The program, established as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, allows individual taxpayers to donate to scholarship-granting organizations in exchange for a federal tax rebate.
articles.takeaway: Governor Hochul announced the state will participate in a federal scholarship tax credit program, aiming to generate funds for public school students.
body: Governor Kathy Hochul announced Friday that New York will opt into a federal scholarship tax credit program, a move she believes will bring millions of dollars to the state for public school students. The program, established as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, allows individual taxpayers to donate to scholarship-granting organizations in exchange for a federal tax rebate.

This decision makes New York one of 30 states to participate in the program. While primarily designed to expand private school choice, it also offers a pathway to raise funds for public school initiatives, particularly tutoring services. Governor Hochul stated that the program has the potential to provide additional resources without diverting funds from existing public school budgets or state and local finances.

The program allows families earning up to 300% of the area median income to qualify for assistance with educational expenses. However, Governor Hochul will not have the authority to dictate which organizations receive funding or to prevent discrimination based on religion or LGBTQ status, nor can she restrict scholarships to low-income students.

The governor's decision has drawn mixed reactions. Some, like United Federation of Teachers President Michael Mulgrew, have criticized the move, calling it a "failure of leadership" and expressing concern over potential impacts on public education. Others, such as Nicole Pollock, president of Democrats for Education Reform, have highlighted the potential benefits for public school students, emphasizing the need to ensure these funds reach families in need.

attribution.originalTitle: New York Is Opting Into Federal Private School Choice Program, Hochul Says

faqs.question: How does the federal scholarship tax credit program work?
faqs.answer: Individual taxpayers can donate up to $1,700 to a scholarship-granting organization and receive a dollar-for-dollar tax rebate from the federal government, with the organization then providing funds to qualifying families for educational expenses.

faqs.question: What are the potential benefits for New York students?
faqs.answer: Governor Hochul believes the program can generate millions of dollars for public school students, potentially funding services like tutoring and speech therapy that schools may not be able to afford.

Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman sparred over immigration policy, President Donald Trump and who deserves blame for the rising cost of living during a 60-minute debate Tuesday night.

Both candidates repeatedly fell back on their campaign talking points during their 60-minute debate at Spectrum News NY1’s studios above Chelsea Market, which marked what may have been their best chance to appeal directly to New York voters three weeks before Election Day.

The debate seemed to lack any major gaffes or viral moments that could meaningfully shift the race. Hochul, the incumbent Democrat, touted her record in office while bringing up Blakeman’s support for Trump no fewer than 10 times, a move she hopes will resonate in a state where polls show most voters have a low opinion of the Republican president.

“This is your choice, New Yorkers,” she said, noting Blakeman once said he wants to bring “Trump-style leadership” to Albany. “I'm not letting this happen.” Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, repeatedly blamed Hochul for rising gas and electric bills across the state.

He said Hochul had made the state less safe through New York’s sanctuary policies for migrants. But he largely shied away from tying Hochul to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other democratic socialists, whom the Republican has used as a boogeyman while campaigning in more moderate and conservative areas of the state.
Blakeman’s strategy has been complicated in recent months by Trump, who has embraced the socialist mayor. “I’m going to ask you to vote for change,” Blakeman said in his opening statement.

articles.headline: New York City Council to Vote on Banning Central Park Carriage Horses
articles.dek: Legislation aims to phase out the industry, with officials promising protections for workers and horses.
articles.lead: The New York City Council is set to vote on legislation that would phase out the city's carriage horse industry in Central Park. Council Speaker Julie Menin announced that the chamber would hold a vote on October 22.
articles.takeaway: Legislation aims to phase out the industry, with officials promising protections for workers and horses.
body: The New York City Council is set to vote on legislation that would phase out the city's carriage horse industry in Central Park. Council Speaker Julie Menin announced that the chamber would hold a vote on October 22.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani stated his support for the ban, vowing that his administration would ensure the safety of workers and horses. Animal rights advocates have long campaigned for an end to the practice, with recent incidents highlighting concerns.

A carriage horse collapsed and died in June, followed by the death of a tourist, Romanch Mahajan, who fell from a runaway carriage horse in the park. Following Mahajan's death, a bill to ban carriage horses was renamed in his honor and a public hearing was held.

While the legislation aims to provide new economic opportunities for displaced drivers, the Transport Workers Union, which represents them, expressed concerns that the bill lacks concrete economic relief. Animal rights group NYCLASS and the Central Park Conservancy have supported the ban.

attribution.originalTitle: NYC Council, Mayor Mamdani agree to end Central Park's carriage horse industry

faqs.question: When will the New York City Council vote on the carriage horse ban?
faqs.answer: The New York City Council is scheduled to hold a vote on October 22.

faqs.question: What protections are planned for workers and horses?
faqs.answer: City officials have stated that the administration will ensure workers and owners are protected and that the horses will be safe, with plans to connect drivers with new economic opportunities.
